title: Bacterial flagellum and the question of what it is to be alive
publication_boundary: This public artifact includes claim summaries, citation metadata, source links, and TOA mappings. It does not publish the full third-party source text, full English working translation, private source captures, local Library paths, or review caches.

claims.summary: The bacterial flagellar motor is described mechanistically as work driven by a proton imbalance across the membrane.
Bacterial flagella are rigid helical filaments rotated by a membrane-embedded motor rather than cilium-like contraction.
Cryo-electron microscopy work reported a 5:2 stator architecture relevant to coupling stator rotation to the C-ring.
A cited PNAS paper is used for a quantitative claim about proton flux through stators and torque generation.
CheY phosphorylation and C-ring binding are presented as mechanisms for rapid motor switching and tumbling.
Chemiosmotic theory explains cellular work as powered by proton gradients rather than a special vital force.
Michael Behe used the bacterial flagellum as a central example of irreducible complexity and intelligent design.
Kitzmiller v. Dover is used for the legal-historical conclusion that intelligent design is religious creationism rather than public-school science.
A 2025 mBio paper is used as evidence that MotAB stators and non-flagellar relatives illuminate flagellar evolutionary history.
The origin of proton gradients in first cells is framed as an open origins-of-life question with alkaline hydrothermal vents as an active research context.

The Krebs (citric-acid/TCA) cycle supplies an independent biochemical example relevant to the docket's blanket irreducible-complexity framing: published work models its opportunistic assembly from pre-existing reactions, while later experiments identify chemically feasible reverse-cycle and precursor networks.
claims.finding: This does not resolve the flagellum's own history and should not be presented as direct flagellar evidence. It does, however, make the general claim that no detailed evolutionary accounts exist for biochemical systems untenable. Exact ancestral order and timing remain open questions.
